Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
Making any plans for the future

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

issues.item: Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
issues.explanation: 'Irritability' is not a threat appraisal/perception item; it reflects arousal/behavioral dysregulation and fits better outside the Threat node. In this profile, the other Threat items are coherent terrorism-related hypervigilance/safety behaviors ('Scanning Exits', 'Back to Wall'), so this item is internally mismatched within the node and weakly aligned with the formulation in which Memory-linked threat should reflect perceived current danger rather than aggressive behavior.

vignette: Kofi had always been proud of his skills as a tailor, taking pleasure in creating beautiful garments that made people feel confident and elegant. But on that fateful day three years ago, everything changed. He was working at the market in downtown Nairobi when a terrorist attack shook the city. Kofi remembered the sound of gunfire and explosions, the screams of the wounded, and the feeling of chaos as people ran for their lives. In the months that followed, Kofi found it increasingly difficult to recall the event without feeling numb, as if he was watching someone else's life unfold. There were parts of that day that remained stubbornly blank, no matter how hard he tried to remember. But other memories haunted him – the image of a young woman crying over her injured child, the smell of smoke and blood, the sound of sirens piercing the air. As Kofi struggled to make sense of what had happened, he began to doubt his own abilities. He couldn't trust that he would do the right thing in a crisis, and this self-doubt seeped into every aspect of his life. He became withdrawn, avoiding social gatherings and events where he might be reminded of the attack. He stopped making plans for the future, unable to envision a life beyond the present moment. Kofi's daily routine became a series of avoidance strategies. He spent hours on his phone, scrolling through social media or playing games, trying to distract himself from the memories that lingered just beneath the surface. He picked arguments with friends and family, creating drama as a way to deflect attention from his own pain. And he stopped making plans for the future – no trips, no goals, no aspirations. But even in the midst of these avoidance strategies, Kofi's hypervigilance remained on high alert. He scanned every room he entered, searching for exits and potential threats. He positioned himself with his back to a wall, where he could see everything happening around him. And he was constantly watchful, waiting for the next attack. As time passed, these habits began to take a toll on Kofi's relationships and work. His friends grew tired of his constant conflict-seeking, and his clients started to notice his distraction and lack of focus. Kofi's shop, once a thriving business, began to falter. Despite this downward spiral, Kofi couldn't shake the feeling that he was weak – that he had somehow failed to protect himself or others during the attack. This weakness belief had become a mantra, echoing in his mind whenever he felt anxious or scared. And it was accompanied by another, equally painful thought: I no longer belong anywhere. It was this sense of disconnection, combined with the weight of his memories and avoidance strategies, that finally brought Kofi to seek help. He couldn't continue living in a state of constant hypervigilance, forever scanning for threats and avoiding plans for the future. He wanted to learn how to live again – to trust himself, to make plans, and to find a sense of belonging in a world that still felt hostile and unforgiving. As Kofi sat in his therapist's office, he looked around the room with a mixture of hope and fear. He was scared of what might happen if he confronted his memories head-on – but he was more afraid of living the rest of his life trapped in this cycle of avoidance and self-doubt.
